title: Intensification and Spatial Reorganization of Drought Risks for Global Rainfed Crops Under Climate Change
content:
Climate and root-zone drought diverge increasingly under warming, escalating global maize, soybean, and wheat production losses. CO2 fertilization partially buffers losses—most strongly for wheat—but amplifies rather than creates this divergence, with severe drought emerging as the dominant future contributor.


ABSTRACT

Rainfed agriculture covers roughly 80% of global cropland and supplies more than half of global food production, yet uncertainty in how meteorological drying propagates into root-zone water deficits and crop losses impedes robust risk assessment. Here, we establish an integrated, production-weighted assessment framework coupling SPEI, SSI, and 12 GGCMI3 crop models to trace how meteorological drying propagates into root-zone deficits and crop losses, explicitly separating affected area, conditional yield loss, and accumulated production loss across rainfed maize, soybean, and wheat. By 2070–2099, opposing-direction SPEI–SSI change classes occupied 6.8%–28.4% of rainfed area across crops under SSP1-2.6/default CO2 and 26.6%–48.2% under SSP5-8.5/default CO2. Comparison with fixed-2015 CO2 experiments (7.5%–27.6% and 21.7%–34.9%, respectively) indicates that elevated CO2 substantially expanded the spatial footprint of this hydrometeorological decoupling. Historically, SSI-defined drought affected 12–16 million ha year−1 and was associated with annual production losses of 5–12 Mt year−1 (1.6–2.0% year−1). Under default CO2, affected area increased to 14–21 million ha under SSP1-2.6 and 19–27 million ha under SSP5-8.5, with production losses of 6–12 and 9–12 Mt year−1, respectively. Under SSP5-8.5, median loss rates were higher under fixed-2015 than default CO2 for maize (3.33 vs. 1.96% year−1), soybean (4.22 vs. 2.84% year−1) and wheat (5.41 vs. 2.90% year−1), as elevated CO2 reduces stomatal water loss and thus mitigates drought impacts, whereas SSP1-2.6 estimates were similar. Severe drought became the largest loss contributor under both pathways and CO2 settings. Under default CO2, loss increases clustered in Central America, northeastern Brazil, western Europe and southern Africa; fixed-2015 CO2 broadened the area of robust grid-cell loss increases. These results show that drought-related production losses are spatially uneven and sensitive to the modeled CO2 response, highlighting the value of crop- and region-specific risk assessment.
